hints: Think about what could or could not influence a nucleus deep inside an atom - would heating, pressure or chemical reactions make any difference to decay?
Think about the difference between predicting the behaviour of a huge sample and predicting a single nucleus - what can you say, and what can you never say, about which nucleus decays next and when?
walkthrough:
**Spontaneous means on its own**
Think of spontaneous as happening without any trigger from outside. The nucleus decays by itself due to its internal instability. Changing temperature, pressure, chemical state or surroundings has no effect on the rate. That is why we say it is spontaneous.

**Random means unpredictable for one nucleus**
Think of random as unpredictable at the level of a single nucleus. For a large sample you can predict the average rate using half-life, but you cannot predict when a particular nucleus will decay or which one will be next. Each nucleus has the same probability of decaying in the next instant.

Final answer: 1. spontaneous decay: decay is not affected by external factors such as temperature, pressure or chemical environment. 2. random decay: it cannot be predicted when a particular nucleus will decay, or which nucleus will decay next.

hints: Start from what you are given - an activity in MBq and a tiny mass in kg. What two quantities must you link to get the decay constant, and which one do you still need to find from the mass?
Use $A = \lambda N$ so $\lambda = A/N$. First convert activity to $\text{Bq}$ ($\text{s}^{-1}$) and find $N$ from mass divided by mass of one Sr-90 nucleus.
Remember nucleon number 90 gives the mass of one nucleus as $90u$, where $u = 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$. Check your powers of ten carefully when dividing.
walkthrough:
**Find the number of nuclei N in the sample**
You have mass $m = 1.0 \times 10^{-9} \text{ kg}$ of Sr-90 with nucleon number 90. One nucleus has mass about $90u$: $$ m_{atom} = 90 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg} = 1.49 \times 10^{-25} \text{ kg} $$ So: $$ N = \frac{m}{m_{atom}} = \frac{1.0 \times 10^{-9}}{90 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27}} \approx 6.7 \times 10^{15} $$ This is the number of undecayed nuclei present.

**Use activity to get decay constant**
Activity is the rate of decay: $$ A = \lambda N $$ Convert $5.2 \text{ MBq}$ to becquerel: $$ A = 5.2 \times 10^{6} \text{ s}^{-1} $$ Rearrange before substituting: $$ \lambda = \frac{A}{N} $$

**Calculate and add the unit**
Substitute values: $$ \lambda = \frac{5.2 \times 10^{6}}{6.7 \times 10^{15}} \approx 7.8 \times 10^{-10} \text{ s}^{-1} $$ The unit $\text{s}^{-1}$ is the same as $\text{Bq}$ per nucleus, showing probability of decay per unit time.
Final answer: $N = 6.7 \times 10^{15}$ nuclei, $A = 5.2 \times 10^{6} \text{ Bq}$, $\lambda = A/N = 7.8 \times 10^{-10} \text{ s}^{-1}$.

hints: After one half-life half the Sr-90 remains, so why would the counter read too high? Think about what the new nuclei formed by the decay might themselves do.
walkthrough:
**Extra counts mean an extra source**
After 1.0 half-life you expect only half the parent Sr-90 activity, about $2.6 \text{ MBq}$. A higher reading means the detector is seeing decays from something else as well. That something is the daughter nuclei produced in the decay. If those daughter nuclei are themselves unstable and radioactive, their decays add to the total measured activity.
Final answer: The daughter / product nucleus formed is also unstable (radioactive) and decays, contributing additional activity to the measured total.
